channel.title: abcodex · release log
channel.description: What is new in abcodex. Daily ingests, prompted batches, depth passes.

item.title: What stays human when generation is cheap
item.description: Five cards, four new operators. Dan Shipper delivers the mechanism at the center of Every's annual thesis conference: generation is now cheap, so ranking and perspective become the scarce skills. Four operators attending the same conference converge on adjacent answers about what that means for work, hiring, product design, and creative expression.

item.title: AI value chain economics and the two optimization myths
item.description: Four cards, three operators. Tom Tunguz publishes two back-to-back posts mapping where AI gross profit actually lives and what Jensen Huang's resignation means for AI capital flows. Kevin Indig and Antoine van der Lee independently surface the same pattern: a common optimization assumption that measurement disproves.

item.title: Proxy failures, measurement gaps, and the limits of learning from a distance
item.description: Four cards, four operators. Ethan Mollick and Aleyda Solis publish from different domains on the same underlying problem: measuring the wrong thing. Thorsten Ball and Chris Zukowski converge on a separate idea that only direct experience reveals true capability, in AI coding and in games.

item.title: AI economics at two scales, and scope discipline in generated systems
item.description: Four cards, two operators. Simon Willison and Tom Tunguz publish from independent angles on how to measure AI costs correctly, where US token supply runs out, and what distinguishes companies that bend trajectories from companies that only move faster. Willison adds a design constraint for LLM-generated data apps.

item.title: Agents expanding their reach, and the judgment gap they still cannot close
item.description: Four cards. Simon Willison (Nov 9) on keeping human editorial judgment visible in AI-generated PR descriptions. Simon Willison (Nov 9) on giving coding agents a sensory channel through browser APIs. Ethan Mollick (Nov 9) on self-evaluation as the new jagged frontier gap. Thorsten Ball (Nov 8) on the SDLC boundary agents can own up to but not past.

item.title: Judgment as scarce resource, and the library function as bottleneck
item.description: Two cards. Ann Handley (Exit Five Podcast #409, Oct 29) on the marketing shift from speed to judgment when AI makes output cheap. Simon Willison (Nov 8) on how a narrow hand-tuned parser outperforms a standard library function regardless of language.

item.title: Performance-based creator pay, the SEO execution gap, and zero-click visitor pre-qualification
item.description: Three cards, one new operator. Hector Serrano (Wispr Flow) on paying UGC creators a share of ad spend as a quality filter. Aleyda Solis on why only 28% of SEO teams implement 80%+ of their own recommendations. Rand Fishkin on conversion rates rising as traffic falls when platforms pre-qualify visitors.

item.title: Power limits AI scale, $90 opens company networks, and LLM alignment verification is fundamentally broken
item.description: Three cards, no new operators. Tom Tunguz's November 4 post yields one card on electrical power as the binding ceiling on 2027 AI compute. His November 6 post yields one card on how AI-agent attacks collapsed enterprise intrusion costs 99% in five months. Sean Goedecke's November 2 post yields one card arguing that knowing whether an LLM is reliably aligned is impossible in principle.

item.title: Engineers become AI team leads, and proxy metrics capture the wrong audience
item.description: Four cards, two new operators. Bart Butler's Proton engineering manifesto yields one card on the engineer's role shift from code writer to AI team leader. Simon Willison's November 3 experiment yields one card on local 27B models interpreting neural network weights. Sean Goedecke yields two cards: one on engagement metrics driving away thoughtful readers, one on noticing as the scarce AI delegation skill.

item.title: AI search displacement forces platform pivots, and verification economics govern model choice
item.description: Four cards, three operators. Eric Seufert's analysis of Reddit's Q3 2026 earnings and Apple's App Store slowdown yields two cards on how AI search displacement changes platform monetization strategy. Simon Willison's llm 0.37 release notes yield one card on absorbing AI-assisted PR floods in open source. Thorsten Ball's October 25 essay yields one card on the false economy of cheaper models when error rate requires universal verification.

item.title: AI lab margin mechanics, channel portfolio under search decline, and trust signal erosion
item.description: Four cards from four operators. Tom Tunguz's November 3 essay on Anthropic's S-1 yields one card on the GPU duration mismatch that will define AI lab margins in 2027. Kevin Indig's November 2 Growth Memo yields one card on email as a floor channel when organic search falls. Ethan Mollick's November Wharton piece yields one card on the verification-cost trap in Conjurer-mode delegation. Kyle Kingsbury's October 31 Jepsen analysis yields one card on LLM-generated docs eroding documentation as a trust signal.

item.title: AI stack economics from four angles, and a broken measurement baseline
item.description: Four cards from two operators. Tom Tunguz's November 2 essay on the four questions of AI yields three cards on stack economics: harness-layer margin mechanics, thin-wrapper mortality, and the double-pendulum coupling across all four layers. Simon Willison's November 2 post on the Census Bureau's survey wording changes yields one card on how the headline AI adoption data broke.

item.title: Training weight resistance, two context failure modes, and the hyperscaler funding race
item.description: Three cards from two operators. Drew Breunig's October 24 essay on context engineering yields two more uncaptured failure modes: training-era priors that resist runtime instructions, and a hallucinated fact embedding itself as an unresolvable goal constraint. Tom Tunguz's October 29 analysis of Q3 hyperscaler earnings maps the race between building a trillion-dollar AI compute business and the yield compression in the legacy cash flows that fund it.

item.title: Agent workflow discipline and AI peer review outperforming human experts
item.description: Five cards from two operators. Thorsten Ball published a 15-point guide to working with coding agents on October 25; four cards pull the most distinct mechanisms. Gary King and Steven Worthington published a Harvard controlled study on October 28 showing Claude Opus 4.8 outperformed paid human expert reviewers on every measured review dimension across 124 papers.

item.title: Context distraction, AI-vs-Google behavioral divergence, and the branding channel reframe
item.description: Four cards from three operators. Drew Breunig names a fifth context failure mode: contradictory examples in chat history override explicit instructions, backed by a 13-model experiment. Cate Dombrowski at iPullRank matches 16,310 users across Google and AI panels and finds 96% of AI prompts have no Google counterpart in the same session. Mike King argues that judging AI search by referral traffic is a category error because AI answers are earned media composed by machines, not click competitors.

item.title: AI game design taste, answer-first AEO, clone defense, AI economics, and the hourly deploy loop
item.description: Five cards from five operators. Simon Willison calls October 2026 the inflection point for vibe coding games, now that models can produce fun gameplay rather than just working code. Mike Taylor runs 2,484-session experiments showing that agents cite answer-first headlines and ignore curiosity framing. Chris Zukowski documents the first AI clone overtaking an original game on Steam, and maps the three conditions that make it happen. Tom Tunguz measures AI application revenue catching up to infrastructure spend twice as fast as the web era did, with a circularity warning. Jacob Sansbury describes Spawn, a game studio where an hour without a production deploy is a SEV-0.

item.title: GitHub volume as agent signal, the expert forecasting gap, and memory as the next agent differentiator
item.description: Three cards from three operators. Simon Willison reads GitHub Octoverse 2026 and finds that code-volume stats now track agent adoption, not human headcount. Ethan Mollick documents the forecasting failure: top predictors gave AI a 2.3% chance of winning the Math Olympiad by 2025. It won in 2025. Harrison Chase names persistent memory as the next defining gap for AI agents.

item.title: Security as AI's third market, and AI company risk as compute commitment
item.description: Two cards from Tom Tunguz, both published October 26. Security joins coding and customer support as AI's third product-market fit, driven by attack parallelization that defense headcount cannot match. Anthropic's S-1 reveals that AI foundation model companies carry their financial risk in long-term compute commitments, not debt.

item.title: Code aesthetics as cognitive artifact, agent pro-tool threshold, and organic decline as a publisher problem
item.description: Four cards across three operators. Thorsten Ball on the working memory origin of code elegance and where full software automation arrives first. Dan Shipper on what makes a personal agent a pro tool. Kevin Indig on how the organic traffic decline story is a publisher story, not a universal one.

item.title: Wednesday is the cliff, percentage growth is the trap, and AI slop already lives at the bottom
item.description: Four cards, one operator, one source. Chris Zukowski's October 2026 Steam Next Fest analysis surfaces how Valve's algorithm actually works, which metrics predict rank, and how AI-disclosed games are already stratifying into the bottom tiers.

item.title: Context engineering's hard split, inference payback, and the cloud-provider frame
item.description: Four cards across two lanes. Drew Breunig maps the core tension in context engineering: what to fix in code versus what to leave to the model. Tomasz Tunguz builds a four-rung GPU revenue ladder showing sub-1-year payback at real-world efficiency levels, then applies cloud-provider multiples to argue Anthropic is being evaluated on the wrong comp set.

item.title: Build-out velocity, quota amplification, and the benchmark that saturated
item.description: Three cards across three lanes. Tomasz Tunguz maps AI's infrastructure build-out against Carlota Perez's model and finds it running twice as fast as the web era. Bardia Shahali shows how AI tools push rep quotas to multiples of prior norms, compressing comp cycles to quarters. Ethan Mollick surfaces METR benchmark data showing AI task duration doubled eight times since GPT-4, from four minutes to 17 hours, before the benchmark itself saturated.

item.title: Identity pages, undirected prompts, and agents that won't let go
item.description: Three cards from three lanes. Lily Ray finds an About page outperforming a homepage 5x in AI Overviews. Simon Willison shows how vague quality directives outperform specific requests in vibe coding. Drew Breunig names the failure mode where agents get stuck and explains why summarization makes it worse.

item.title: Conjurers, thresholds, arcade money, and what programmers mourn
item.description: Four cards from three lanes. Ethan Mollick names a third AI work mode. Hamel Husain shows why the default 0.50 eval threshold silently fails. Elena Verna diagnoses AI pricing as arcade money. Simon Willison splits the programming profession by what it valued.

item.title: Build a Lab, resist automation, and fix the broken apprenticeship ladder
item.description: Three cards from Ethan Mollick's October 18 Charter interview. The Leadership-Crowd-Lab model for organizational AI structure, the case against automation-first strategy, and why AI is collapsing the junior talent development path.

item.title: Agents split programmer value, AI-direct attribution stays broken, and chatbot gains stay individual
item.description: Three cards. Simon Willison on how LLMs redistribute value within programming. Kevin Indig on why GA4 correlation analysis cannot isolate AI search's contribution to Direct traffic. Ethan Mollick on why individual AI productivity gains do not automatically aggregate to organizational performance.

item.title: Production gates, chip economics, and the collapse of the consideration set
item.description: Five cards from four operators across three lanes. Thorsten Ball on pushing to main with no code review. Tomasz Tunguz on chip ownership as the AI cost floor and security's rise to the top enterprise pain point. Ethan Mollick on the four human attributes that remain valuable. Kevin Indig on AI Mode accepting as-is at 88%.

item.title: Swarm direction, proactive catches, and quality goals in prompts
item.description: Three cards from two operators across two lanes. Ethan Mollick on how direction replaces coordination as the bottleneck in agent swarms and on what proactive personal agents catch that responsive chatbots miss. Simon Willison on how explicitly stating a quality goal in a creative coding prompt produces polish that functional specs alone cannot.

item.title: Review before the PR exists, and structure before AI generates content
item.description: Four cards from two operators across two lanes. Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang on moving code review to writing-time and using multi-agent consensus to gate findings. Alex Cornell on chain-of-thought display as a latency workaround and fixed-structure-dynamic-content as the reliable generative UI pattern.

item.title: Custom silicon moats, the post-purchase AI loop, and audience context over audience size
item.description: Four cards from four operators across three lanes. Tom Tunguz on hardware as the AI cost moat and the security tooling gap in enterprise AI. Kevin Indig on post-purchase signals driving AI search shortlist position. Jake Castillo on influencer audience context determining app conversion.
